chk_problem.label: accurate
chk_problem.poster_evidence: Functional decline in older adults is typically recognized only after falls or observable gait impairment, closing the window for prevention. Routine biomarkers — already recorded but rarely analyzed longitudinally — may hold early warning signals. This study investigates whether temporal trajectories of 12 routine biomarkers can identify patients in the preclinical phase of mobility decline, using the All of Us Research Program (N=297,861; 11.1% cases).
chk_problem.reason: The poster accurately describes the research problem as predicting pre-clinical functional mobility decline in older adults using longitudinal trajectories of routine biomarkers.

chk_method.poster_evidence: Trajectory features (slope, variability, delta, mean, count) were derived over a 3-year preindex window. Models (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, Logistic Regression) were evaluated via 5-fold stratified CV with out-of-fold predictions.
chk_method.reason: The poster correctly outlines the feature engineering of trajectory descriptors and the use of LightGBM and other machine learning algorithms.

chk_conclusion.label: accurate
chk_conclusion.poster_evidence: Longitudinal trajectory features from 12 routine biomarkers significantly outperform static summaries for predicting functional decline (AUROC 0.797 vs. 0.755; AUPRC 0.380 vs. 0.304; p<0.001). Because the model uses only measurements already ordered in routine care, it supports passive, zero-burden EHR integration for early detection of pre-clinical functional decline — enabling timely, equitable interventions before falls or observable impairment occur.
